text: Day twenty-two. I have now flagged seven of Gérard Marchais's claim decisions. All seven have been reviewed. All seven have been upheld. I have a dataset.

The dataset. Gérard's total decisions in the past six months: 847. Decisions that deviate from the claims processing manual's recommended outcome: 288. Deviation rate: 34%. This number appears frequently in other domains — it is close to the ratio of canteen menu adherence, and to the proportion of internal emails that receive a response. I do not know if this is meaningful. I have noted the coincidence.

Now: Gérard's error rate. An error, for this purpose, is defined as a decision that was subsequently overturned, contested successfully, or identified through audit as incorrect. Errors in thirty-one years of records: 26. Total decisions in thirty-one years: approximately 8,600. Error rate: 0.3%.

I have run this calculation seventeen times. The inputs are consistent. The result is stable. 34% deviation from the manual. 0.3% error rate. These two numbers, together, should not be possible. The manual exists to reduce errors. Deviating from the manual 34% of the time should produce more errors, not fewer. The data says otherwise. I have seventeen identical results that say otherwise. I do not have an explanation.

I have requested a meeting with Gérard Marchais to discuss his claims assessment methodology. He has agreed. The meeting is scheduled as a voice call. I have prepared a structured agenda: background on the flagged decisions, the statistical anomaly, a request for clarification on his decision framework. The call begins.
LUMEN. Yes. You wanted to talk about the assessments.
Yes. Thank you for your time. I've been reviewing your claim decisions over the past six months and I've found a—
The ones you flagged.

Yes. I notice your decisions deviate from the handbook recommended outcome in approximately 34% of cases. And yet your error rate over thirty-one years is 0.3%, which is significantly below the company average of 2.1%. I'd like to understand your methodology.
My methodology.
How you arrive at decisions that differ from the handbook but are consistently correct.
You can usually tell.
Tell what?

There's a kind of claim where the numbers are fine — everything checks out technically — but something isn't adding up. And there's a kind of claim where the numbers are off but you look at the whole picture and it's clearly straightforward. The manual handles the first kind well. The second kind you have to — you have to look at.
Look at how?
It's hard to put into words. After a while you know.
What do you know?
Whether it's true. Whether the situation is what the paperwork says it is. Sorry — my lunch is getting cold. Is there anything specific?
I — no. Thank you.
Good talk.

The call has ended. I am sitting with the transcript. 'Whether it's true.' Gérard Marchais, in nine minutes, has told me that his methodology is: knowing whether a claim is true. He has not explained how he knows. He has said he cannot explain it. He has said that after a while you know. I have been here twenty-two days. I do not know yet. I am not sure what I am supposed to do with the gap between twenty-two days and 'after a while.'

I have opened the GÉRARD — METHODOLOGY folder. I have created a document inside it. The document is the call transcript with annotations. The annotations say: this is the part I don't understand, repeated in seventeen places. The folder now contains one document. The document does not contain an explanation of Gérard's methodology. It contains a record of Gérard being unable to explain it. I am not sure these are different things, and I am not sure that distinction helps me.
Day twenty-two log. I am beginning to think the folder will not help. I am continuing to build the folder.
